newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African central bank to monitor Telkom inflows.
newsitem.headline: S.African central bank to monitor Telkom inflows.

text.p: South Africa's central bank will be monitoring closely the inflow of $1.26 billion in proceeds from the part privatisation of Telkom and may take action to offset the resulting increase in money market liquidity.

"The decision on the extent to which the inflow will be counteracted will be taken closer to the time and will depend on market conditions and the economic cycle," Business Day newspaper quoted Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals as saying.
"The Bank can use intruments such as Treasury bills and currency swaps to mop up the liquidity."

The cash is expected to flow into the money market within the next three months. Officials say the money will be paid by the U.S.-Malaysian consortium acquiring the 30 percent stake on finalisation of the deal, expected within 90 days of the signing on March 26.

The bulk of the inflow from the sale of the stake in the state-run telecomunications concern is expected to affect the money market, as Telkom's bank accounts are in the private sector, Business Day said.
The timing of the inflow may be fortuitous since it will likely coincide with government moves to ease foreign exchange controls on individuals from July 1, which could lead to an outflow of funds.

South Africa's daily money market shortage has remained around 10 billion rand in recent months and Stals has said on several occasions he is happy to see it remain high in order to deter banks for over-extending credit.
SBC Communications Inc will pay 60 percent of the $1.26 billion bill for the strategic stake in Telkom with Telekom Malaysia Bhd paying 40 percent.
The deal, the first major sell-off of state assets in South Africa and the largest direct investment in the country to date, values Telkom at $4.2 billion.
Of the proceeds, $1 billion will be injected back into Telkom to help fund its infrastructure expansion programme and the balance will go to the state to cut government debt.
